speaker: michaelrobertson
text: Thank you, Sage. And thank you all for having me. Dear Mayor Clark, members of the Norman City Council and Human Rights Commissioners, respect for human decency and development of scientific-based policy should be cornerstones of democracy. Government has an obligation to provide protections for citizens and is particularly accountable for vulnerable populations. Norman has stood as a beacon of hope for the LGBTQ plus individuals. It is a place that welcomes and celebrates diversity, but it must take a firm stand for the rights of LGBTQ plus youth by banning sexual orientation change efforts and so-called conversion therapy. Since 1998, the American Psychiatric Association has opposed the use of conversion therapy. The APA bases their opposition on the long-withstanding knowledge that identifying as LGBTQ plus is not a mental disorder. Attempts to change an individual's sexuality or gender identity are not only futile and ineffective, they're also extremely dangerous. As of the writing of this letter, all major counseling associations, including the American Counseling Association, National Association of Social Workers, and the American Association for Marriage and Family Therapists have renounced this harmful practice. Many professionals in a community strongly oppose the term conversion therapy, instead preferring the term sexual orientation change efforts. Those who provide therapeutic mental health services feel that the word therapy should be reserved for services that heal. Sexual orientation change efforts often lead to increased self-esteem issues, self-harm, and even more severe consequences, including increased substance abuse, suicidal ideation, and risky behaviors. Not only is there no credible evidence that conversion therapy methods of any kind actually work, there is a large amount of data that proves its ineffectiveness. Therefore, it comes into question why there are calls for supporting and validating such harmful practices, especially considering that all major counseling and psychology, excuse me, I'll back up. Therefore, it comes into question why there are calls for supporting and validating such harmful practices, especially considering that all major counseling and psychological organizations and most professionals in the field speak so strongly against it. Sexual orientation change efforts continue to exist due to an ill-informed public with biases and fears filling their hearts and minds. Any professionals who practice these efforts and those who support them in their use are continuing to stigmatize and attempting to erase LGBTQ plus individuals. We cannot stand by while state lawmakers attempt to lay claim to the lives of children on the grounds of parental and religious rights. History has its eyes on us. Norman again has the opportunity to be on the right side of history, to be a safe haven of hope and love. But this is not just about optics and symbolism, it is about protecting children from reckless and harmful practices. Therefore, we ask that an ordinance be passed to prohibit the licensed professionals from practicing conversion therapy on our LGBTQ plus youth in the city of Norman. Sincerely, Norman Pride Board and Norman P. Flagg Board of Directors.

speaker: nathanielsmith
text: Good evening. So let me get this pulled up real quick and we will get started. Alrighty. So I'm gonna go a little bit more in depth into exactly what conversion therapy is. So as defined by the Trevor Project, conversion therapy is the pseudoscientific practice of trying to change an individual's sexual orientation or gender identity. There is no reliable evidence that sexual orientation can be changed and medical institutions warn that conversion therapy practices are ineffective and potentially harmful. According to a 2009 report of the American Psychological Association, the techniques that therapists have used to try to change sexual orientation and gender identity include inducing nausea, vomiting, paralysis, all while showing patients homoerotic images. Other tactics include providing electrical shocks, having the individual snap an elastic band around the wrist when aroused by same-sex erotic images or thoughts. Techniques also can include trying to make patient's behavior more stereotypically feminine or masculine, teaching heterosexual dating skills, using hypnosis to try to redirect desires. And all of these are based on the scientifically discredited premise that being LGBTQ is a defect. Some may ask, does it work? And simply put, it does not. It is based on an outdated and false notion that being LGBTQ is a mental illness that needs to be cured, despite all major medical associations' agreement that having an LGBTQ identity is a normal variant of human nature. The American Psychiatric Association has not treated homosexuality as a mental illness since 1973. And a 2009 report by the American Psychological Association Task Force found scientifically valid research indicates that it is unlikely that individuals will be able to reduce same-sex attractions or increase other sexual attractions through sexual orientation change efforts. And this is just a very small list of some of the organizations that have denounced the practice of conversion therapy. I could go on for more, but the slide just is not big enough for that. And some of the harms of conversion therapy, it can be extremely dangerous. And in 2009, the APA issued a report concluding that the reported risk of the practices can include depression, guilt, helplessness, shame, social withdrawal, substance abuse, disappointment, self-blame, decreased self-esteem, increased self-hatred, blame towards the parents, feeling of anger and betrayal, problems in sexual and emotional intimacy, high-risk sexual behaviors, and the feeling of being dehumanized and untrue to oneself. And some of the reasons why we need to protect our LGBTQ youth, as you can see from some of the statistics on the screen, it's just a staggering number of LGBTQ youth that is being subjected to this conversion therapy. And as of right now, 0% of our LGBTQ youth in Oklahoma is being protected from conversion therapy. Currently in the US, there are 20 states that have laws that ban conversion therapy. And passing this ordinance would make Norman the first city and the only city in Oklahoma to be protecting their LGBTQ youth. So we conducted some research of local mental health providers in Norman, and six out of the 10 practice or condone the use of conversion therapy. Your decision on this gives Norman the opportunity to be the first and only city in Oklahoma to start protecting its LGBTQ youth. And passing this ordinance would put Norman one step further into building an inclusive community. And now I'm gonna pass on to Pixie, and she's going to go a little bit deeper into the research.

text: Okay, so I wanna begin by saying that the National Center for Lesbian Rights has advised us not to disclose the names of specific locations or providers, and to just focus on the task at hand. text: All right, so I'm just gonna run down through the memo and the ordinance changes in effect. And I'm gonna mention ahead of time, I guess when I sent the materials out for the council conference, I included that previous draft. I'm gonna share my screen. But before I like talk specifically about the ordinance, I kind of wanted to talk more generally about why we went with the approach that we did. And so, and there are two general approach that states have adopted. And I think about 21 states have currently adopted bans on conversion therapy. The majority of which have already established licensing schemes in which they license mental health professionals. And most of them have gone with, I guess you would call it a ban that incorporates it into their state's licensing scheme. So for example, and the one that was introduced in Oklahoma that legislation would have made it unprofessional conduct to engage in any such practice. And so a lot of the times you see, they adopt, I guess what you could call it the California approach because they're the ones who first did it. And so it's through the licensing scheme of mental health providers. The minority approach, only two states have done this way. They have done a use of funds approach. And so they specifically have adopted legislation that restricts state funds for use. And I guess to anyone who's providing these services or putting state funds towards those purposes in and of itself. So that's the minority approach at the state level. And states where they have enacted these bans and states where they haven't enacted these bans, municipalities have also taken it upon themselves to enact local legislation. A lot of these make it a civil fine to engage in these practices. Or they, and this is probably more relevant in states that have a statewide ban as well as, but on the local level in those states, a lot of municipalities have made it, have banned it, but they have their remedy when they actually find a violation of that city ordinance is to refer it to the state agency that licensed those mental health professionals. So it's different from the state statute, but it kind of just sends them back to the state level. So it's not really a local enforcement so much as just local referral to state services. So with all that being said, in order to, in determining which one to approach on the city level, we went with the use of funds approach. That is the minority approach, but I thought that it was the better approach based on the fact that as a municipality, we do not have a mental health licensing scheme and we probably would be easily preempted had we adopted one. And then also, and we could have technically done what other cities have done, which is just outlawed it, I guess. And then, but the difference is we don't, in Oklahoma, we don't really have as a municipality, the alternative to do a civil fine rather than a criminal fine. So technically, a violation of that statute would have been a criminal misdemeanor, which carries higher constitutional protections and wouldn't be as easily enforceable as like a civil fine that other states and other cities have access to and have the procedures to do that. And so our state law just isn't set up for those civil fines at the local level. So based on that, we went with the use of funds approach. And I think that considering Oklahoma law and considering the powers that municipalities have and the constraints that municipalities have in Oklahoma as compared to other states, this is the best approach considering all those factors. And then we incorporated this change into chapter seven, which is the human rights code of the city of Norman. And really the only changes we've made to chapter seven was one, we included a definition of conversion therapy. And then finally, in which I'm gonna share my screen on this. And so on this one, let me kind of, this is the actual language that we would use that restricts the use of city funds. So again, we're limiting it only to mental health providers have all states have done, and we're doing that. So any, the city would not apply, donate or use funds to any mental health provider who's licensed by the state if they engage in conversion therapy for anyone under the age of 18 or anyone who's under a conservatorship, which is just like a guardianship kind of situation. So that's, I'm trying to stop sharing my screen. There it is, okay. And that's kind of the approach and that's kind of the reason why we went with that approach. It's not necessarily the type of conversion therapy ban that most people probably just immediately think of, it's not necessarily the most intuitive approach, but I think it's might be the smartest approach considering the constraints that we're operating under. So, and that's all I have.
